summary.oneLiner: EIH Limited, the flagship company of The Oberoi Group, is a nine-decade-old luxury hospitality operator running Oberoi Hotels & Resorts and Trident Hotels across 30 hotels, resorts and cruisers in six countries.

The portfolio spans Indian gateway cities, palace/heritage and wildlife destinations, and international locations across the Middle East, Africa, Indian Ocean and …

currentContext.strengths: Brand equity built over nine decades under The Oberoi Group, generating pricing power through guest loyalty rather than volume-driven occupancy|Operates with industry-leading margins and zero net debt|Global recognition: Michelin Key designations at five hotels and ranked in the top two of Travel+Leisure World's Best rankings, with exceptional guest satisfaction scores|Diversified and distinct portfolio spanning gateway cities, palace/heritage, wildlife and beach destinations across six countries, which cushioned the year's travel disruption|Resilient domestic demand base across leisure, corporate and event-led segments|Operational leverage on a largely fixed cost base, converting rate growth into above-industry margin performance|CARE AA+ (Stable) issuer rating reflecting a strong credit profile and prudent capital management|Dual-brand architecture (Oberoi luxury, Trident upper-upscale) allowing coverage of both luxury and business/leisure demand pools

13 hotels and restaurants, 7 business units and 4 offices - with quantitative information for the previous year restated to the current reporting boundary|Limited level of external assurance obtained on the BRSR 9 Core Attributes from DNV Business Assurance India Private Limited|Women constitute 33.33% of the Board of Directors|Workforce structure disclosed transparently: no permanent workers, with all workers hired through third-party vendors, and permanent-employee turnover of 42% in FY 2025-26 versus 33% in FY 2024-25|CSR is applicable under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, with a Board-level CSR Committee formulating policy and initiatives|Grievance redressal mechanisms in place for communities, shareholders/investors, employees and workers, and customers - supported by the Oberoi Code of Conduct, POSH policy, Stakeholder Engagement Policy and Whistle-Blower Policy, plus SCORES and ODR portals for shareholders
currentContext.expansion: EIH describes itself as at an inflection point with the most ambitious expansion programme in its history: 29 properties are under development across India, the Middle East, Africa and South Asia, a pipeline that will add approximately 2,500 keys by Calendar Year 2030 and broaden both geographic reach and brand coverage. Management frames this as growth that can be delivered without diluting standards, given industry-leading margins and zero net debt. Alongside new-build expansion, the Company continued to invest in asset improvement during FY 2025-26 - depreciation rose because of hotel renovations and the addition of a new hotel property during the year - and the Directors' Report describes the year's capital expenditure outlay (standalone and consolidated) as reflecting continued investments in expansion and asset improvement initiatives. Funding capacity is supported by nil long-term and short-term borrowings as at 31st March 2026 and a CARE AA+ (Stable) issuer rating assigned during the year.
currentContext.mdna: India is significantly underpenetrated on hotel supply, particularly in the luxury and upper-upscale segments; in many destinations demand continues to outpace the supply of quality accommodation, supporting pricing power|Occupancies remained broadly stable while average room rates strengthened, resulting in another year of RevPAR growth for the Indian hospitality industry|Growing diversity of demand beyond established gateway cities towards heritage destinations, wildlife circuits, wellness retreats, pilgrimage centres and leisure markets such as Khajuraho, Kabini, Coorg, Hampi and Makaibari|Structural demand tailwinds from rising affluence, improving infrastructure, expanding air connectivity and increasing formalisation of the economy|Sharp expansion at the top end of India's income pyramid is enlarging the addressable market and shifting luxury hospitality from an occasional milestone purchase to a recurring lifestyle preference|Geographic decentralisation of affluence into smaller cities (Ahmedabad, Surat, Jaipur, Lucknow, Nagpur, Vadodara, Visakhapatnam) is creating new feeder channels across business travel, leisure, destination weddings and MICE|Policy and connectivity tailwinds: extended Modified UDAN scheme, Seaplane Viability Gap Funding covering destinations in EIH's existing and planned portfolio, PM Gati Shakti, Vande Bharat expansion and proposed high-speed rail corridors|WTTC ranks India the world's 8th largest travel and tourism economy, with tourism's share of GDP still below potential, leaving headroom for sector expansion|Near-term headwind: escalation of the West Asia conflict restructured trans-continental aviation routes, roughly doubling airfares on key Europe-Asia routes, with Indian foreign tourist arrivals declining approximately 20% in the months following escalation; India's domestic travel base provides insulation, with inbound weakness concentrated in Agra, Jaipur and Kerala|Global luxury travel is shifting from amenity-based propositions towards bespoke, culturally embedded experiences, rewarding operators with genuine local depth and service heritage; travellers allocate budget to fewer, longer, more immersive trips, supporting room-rate growth even where occupancy is below peak|Management notes the operating environment in FY 2025-26 was challenging, with geopolitical tensions, West Asia developments, an extended monsoon and aviation disruption negatively influencing demand at different points in the year|Managed hotel development pipeline comprises twenty-four hotels with approximately 1,800 keys|Owned and invested portfolio pipeline includes approximately 825 keys across multiple projects|Pipeline spans a diverse range of destinations across India and international markets, described as one of the strongest pipelines of new hotels in the Company's history

risks.note: Operation Sindhoor in Q1 and the continuing West Asia conflict in Q4 raised global uncertainty; management flags that resulting volatility may hit business sentiment and travel demand in FY 2026-27, with airspace disruption and near-term risk to premium travel flows explicitly called out in the outlook.

Higher fuel prices may influence airline capacity, airfares and travel patterns, in turn affecting inbound foreign tourism and corporate travel - particularly in the historic peak H2 - while elevated fuel and energy prices directly raise operating costs.

risks.risk: Regulatory change - the new Labour Codes
risks.note: Notification of the Code on Wages, Industrial Relations Code, Code on Social Security and OSH Code consolidated multiple labour laws; the Company recognised an incremental obligation for past-service employee benefits as an exceptional item and must continue to absorb further rules, clarifications or amendments.

Cyber risk is one of the thirteen key risk areas identified by the risk framework; the Company handles personal and sensitive guest data and relies on ERP-driven systems, vendors and third-party service providers, making system resilience and access control central to operations.

risks.risk: Operating leverage on a largely fixed cost base
risks.note: Margin performance is delivered through pricing discipline and operational leverage on a largely fixed cost base - the same structure that amplifies earnings on rate growth magnifies the downside if occupancy or rate softens.

The luxury segment faces a structural talent deficit (the policy response being the National Institute of Hospitality); EIH's permanent-employee turnover was 42% in FY 2025-26 (up from 33%), and the workforce constitutes no permanent workers - all workers are hired through third-party vendors.

risks.risk: Broad enterprise risk spectrum overseen by the RMC
risks.note: Thirteen key risk areas have been identified spanning business and financial exposures as well as operational, environmental, reputational, legal and cyber risks; oversight sits with the Risk Management Committee, a Risk Management Sub-Committee chaired by Mr. Arjun Singh Oberoi with Mr. Vikramjit Singh Oberoi as Co-Chair, and a Chief Risk Officer, Mr. Manish Singh.

risks.risk: Technology disruption in travel discovery and booking
risks.note: AI is reshaping how travel is discovered, planned and booked - 80% of Indian travellers already use AI-powered tools - elevating the strategic importance of digital real estate, predictive data architectures and frictionless direct booking; the Company is responding through its ITNext transformation roadmap.

one-line thesis: Highest-ever EBITDA in a genuinely disrupted year (Op Sindoor, West Asia war, monsoon, Dec airline disruptions) — full-year RevPAR +10–12% driven entirely by ARR (+9–10%), occupancy roughly flat; near-term owned-key growth is thin (FY27–28 mostly ARR + ramp-ups) until Oberoi Grand Kolkata (FY28) and a large 825-key owned + 1,893-key managed pipeline land by 2030.
financial scorecard:
**Consolidated Q4FY26:** Revenue +10% YoY; EBITDA only +1% (business-mix change — higher OFS share, higher Q4 expenses, wage-code impact); PAT down (tax impact).
**Standalone Q4FY26:** Revenue +14%; EBITDA flat (mix + higher expenses + wage code); PAT down on prior-year one-time Mashobra fair-value base — but PAT grew from Rs 159 Cr (FY24) to Rs 200 Cr.
**Consolidated FY26 (12M):** Revenue +8%; EBITDA +3% (mix, higher OFS, OAS business absent vs LY, higher admin/other expenses); PAT lower on two one-offs — Rs 30 Cr one-time wage-code + Mashobra fair-value impact (June). Excluding one-timers, profit +2% YoY.
**Standalone FY26:** Revenue grew; EBITDA low single-digit; PAT hit by Mashobra exceptional + wage code.

**Operating KPIs:**
- Owned-hotel full-year occupancy: **76.8–77%**; FY26 RevPAR (owned) **~Rs 17,400**, +8.5% YoY.
- Owned-hotel ARR Q4: **Rs 24,548 → Rs 28,198**; all-domestic (incl. managed) ARR Q4 **Rs 23,648 → Rs 26,536**.
- Industry Q4 occupancy 67–69% (below LY, West Asia war from end-Feb); industry ARR +6–8%, RevPAR +5–7%. FY industry: occupancy ~flat, ARR +9–10%, RevPAR +10–12%.
- Oberoi (luxury) RevPAR: Q4 +4.2% (drag from Oberoi Rajgarh ramp-up; luxury segment +6%); FY +10.4% vs Indian luxury seg +6.4%. RGI 204 (Q4), 191 (FY) — both above LY.
- Trident (upper-upscale): FY RevPAR +10.2% vs segment +5%.
- International RevPAR Q4 **+13%** (Mauritius, Oberoi Zahra, Sahl Hasheesh).
- STR: 13 of 15 hotels ranked #1/#2 (7 first, 6 second).
- FY26 owned room revenue Rs 1,216 Cr; F&B (hotels only, ex-OFS) Rs 670 Cr. OFS Q4 revenue ~Rs 145 Cr.
- Foreign:domestic mix ~50:50 in Q4 (historic); domestic share rose substantially in March.

**Cash / funds flow:** Cash funds **Rs 1,335 Cr** (vs Rs 1,051 Cr at Mar-25). FY26 CFO Rs 993 Cr; investment income Rs 113 Cr; capex Rs 680 Cr; dividends paid Rs 97 Cr. Net cash positive, no debt issue flagged.
guidance (critical):
- **No forward RevPAR/ARR numbers given** (policy). Levers on existing inventory = (1) drive ARR via premium positioning, (2) eliminate waste (not blunt cost-cutting). Mgmt sees "headroom in ARR if market remains buoyant."
- **Apr–May FY27:** "better than expected," led by strong domestic demand (qualitative only).
- **Demand structure:** domestic luxury propensity rising; India underpriced vs Europe/N. America/Asia at top-end luxury ($1,000+ rates common abroad, EIH "well below"); FX devaluation (~15–20%) pushes Indians to travel domestically — tailwind.
- **Supply view:** most luxury industry supply lands FY29–FY30; mgmt not concerned — uses conservative IRR/NPV underwriting, maintains rate premium rather than discounting; demand-supply gap favorable "next couple of years" (CFO).
- **Capex guidance:** ~Rs 600–700 Cr/yr for next 1–2 years; steps up higher toward FY29–30 as bigger hotels come on. Maintenance/replacement capex embedded.
- **Big diplomatic summit expected Q2/Q3 FY27** → some demand benefit (cf. AI Summit boost in Feb/Mar).
order book & pipeline (new hotels / keys:
**Owned pipeline:** +825 keys by 2030. Developed via EIH, EIH Associated Hotels, and Svara (7 hotels total).
- Trident Vizag — opens 2027 (via EIH Associated).
- Oberoi Grand Kolkata — renovation underway; ~200 keys returning, partial opening targeted Sep (sticking to timeline for now); structural issues discovered in old building. Fast ramp-up expected (cf. Oberoi New Delhi reopened post-20-month reno, GOP ~Rs 65 Cr → ~2–3x).
- Hebbal (Bangalore, 8-acre lake site): mixed-use ~1.3M sq ft total — Oberoi hotel + Trident hotel + commercial/F&B/retail (deck cites ~7.63 lakh sq ft commercial). First mixed-use development for EIH; by 2030.
- Other owned: Oberoi Gandikota (delayed from 2028 → 2030 on site relocation for better gorge views); Tirupati (substitute land allotted, redesign underway); plus Goa, London.

**Managed pipeline:** +24 hotels / **1,893 keys** (mostly domestic, some international). Includes 5 Trident managed hotels = 720 keys by 2030 (Goa, Dehradun, Rishikesh + two newly signed: **Amritsar 150-key Trident** and **Pawna Lake 150-key Trident**, both signed Q3–Q4 FY26).

**Current footprint:** 3,800 keys domestic (incl. Rajgarh added Q3) + 400 international keys.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Owned (EIH standalone):** core luxury Oberoi + Trident city/leisure. FY occupancy ~77%, RevPAR ~Rs 17,400.
- **EIH Associated Hotels (associate):** Trident Vizag, Trident Udaipur (kept separate in renovation discussion).
- **OFS (Oberoi Flight Services / flight catering):** Q4 ~Rs 145 Cr, growing on higher flights + larger share of existing/domestic airlines; lower-margin, dilutes blended EBITDA margin and drives airport-levy expense.
- **International:** Mauritius, Oberoi Zahra & Madina (Nile cruisers, Egypt), Sahl Hasheesh (Egypt), Indonesia/Bali (Australia-driven), Morocco. Q4 RevPAR +13%; some West Asia overflight benefit (Egypt/Morocco routes avoid Iran).
- **Mashobra:** O&M contract valid 6 months, running till Oct-26; legal case settled (June); no further P&L impact expected beyond settled items.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Asset-light management:** 1,893-key managed pipeline; two new Trident management contracts (Amritsar, Pawna) signed this year. Fee income scales without owned capex.
- **Mixed-use real estate:** Hebbal Bangalore (hotels + commercial) — new optionality lever, prime location, larger scale than existing Gurgaon ~100–110k sq ft commercial tower.
- **International expansion:** London (under construction), existing geographies; FX/geopolitics-resilient mix.
- **OFS scale-up:** growing with domestic airline volume.
- **Renovation-led uplift:** reopenings (Oberoi Grand) act as quasi-new growth without greenfield risk.
margins & cost dynamics:
- EBITDA growth lagged revenue (Q4 cons. +1% vs +10% rev; FY +3% vs +8%) on: (1) **business-mix shift** — higher OFS (lower margin), (2) **wage-code impact** (Rs 30 Cr one-time FY), (3) higher Q4 expenses — airport levy (OFS), repair & maintenance, CSR, legal expenses, donations; other expenses +20% in Q4.
- Margin philosophy: protect guest/team/asset quality; "eliminate waste," not cut costs. FY27 should normalize (FY25 base had lounge-services + Oberoi Grand drag now lapped; OFS margin base found).
- Rate-premium strategy: won't discount ARR to chase occupancy.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- FY26 capex Rs 680 Cr: Mumbai leasehold→freehold land conversion ~Rs 330 Cr; Oberoi Rajgarh Palace ~Rs 125 Cr (commissioned); ~Rs 100 Cr renovations (Kolkata + others); remainder replacement capex.
- FY27 renovations (EIH): ~<90 rooms Oberoi Bangalore (blocks of 18 over summer); Trident BKC F&B revamp (later in year); 4 floors Trident Nariman Point (~6 months, underway); 4 floors Oberoi Bombay (one floor at a time, staggered) — impact managed in lean months, "minimal."
- **Slippage flagged:** managed-hotel pipeline pushed toward FY29–30 (owner-controlled, EIH doesn't execute); Gandikota slipped 2028→2030. Owned-hotel dates per deck; FY27 owned additions thin.
capital allocation:
- Net-cash: funds Rs 1,335 Cr (up from Rs 1,051 Cr). Self-funds capex from CFO (Rs 993 Cr) + investment income (Rs 113 Cr).
- Dividends paid Rs 97 Cr in FY26.
- Capex Rs 600–700 Cr/yr near-term, stepping up FY29–30; comfortably internally funded.
risks & watch-items:
- **Geopolitics / inbound demand:** West Asia war (from end-Feb) hit foreign room-nights & occupancy in March; higher airfares, fewer routes, Bangalore foreign bookings down. ~50% of Q4 business is foreign — material sensitivity. Mgmt didn't quantify the loss (offset by domestic).
- **Air-quality publicity:** negative international press on North India winter air quality cited as likely cause of weak January (-6% RevPAR).
- **Connectivity dependence:** Oberoi Rajgarh (Khajuraho) — only seasonal Delhi flights (none Jul–Sep), constrains occupancy ramp.
- **Supply wave FY29–30:** luxury micro-markets could see occupancy/ARR pressure (mgmt downplays).
- **Execution slippage** on managed contracts (owner-driven) and owned project redesigns (Gandikota, Tirupati).
- **Margin drag** from rising OFS mix and wage code recurring.
- **Udaipur** weddings down YoY.
management quality / tone: Candid and measured. Vikram Oberoi openly admitted not validating the January demand hypothesis, declined to give forward revenue/3–5yr CAGR ("analysts should model that"), and was self-deprecating (apologized repeatedly for misnaming a participant). Emphasized conservative underwriting (IRR/NPV, sensitivities), rate-premium discipline, and protecting quality over cost-cutting. Credible, owner-operator long-termism; transparent about slippages and structural issues at Oberoi Grand. Tone cautiously confident despite a "very challenging year."
non-obvious takeaways:
- **Highest-ever EBITDA despite the worst-disruption year** — demonstrates ARR-led pricing power and demand resilience.
- **Growth is ARR-led, not key-led, through FY28** — owned inventory roughly static until Oberoi Grand (FY28, ~200 keys); model the next two years on rate + ramp-ups, not new supply.
- **Renovation reopenings ≈ growth engine** — Oberoi New Delhi precedent (GOP ~Rs 65 Cr → 2–3x) is the template for Oberoi Grand Kolkata; faster ramp than greenfield due to brand recognition.
- **OFS is a margin-dilutive but revenue-accretive swing factor** — explains the revenue/EBITDA divergence; airport levy scales with it.
- **FX is a structural tailwind** — rupee devaluation makes outbound 15–20% costlier, redirecting Indian luxury spend domestically.
- **India luxury still "underpriced"** vs global — $1,000+ ARR normal abroad, EIH "well below"; long runway for rate.
- **Hebbal mixed-use** is an under-appreciated optionality (~1.3M sq ft, first such project).
- **Mashobra** O&M de-risked: case settled June, runs only till Oct-26 — no further drag.

segment / subsidiary detail:

- **EIH Associated Hotels (associate):** Trident Vizag, Trident Udaipur (kept separate in renovation discussion).
- **OFS (Oberoi Flight Services / flight catering):** Q4 ~Rs 145 Cr, growing on higher flights + larger share of existing/domestic airlines; lower-margin, dilutes blended EBITDA margin and drives airport-levy expense.
- **International:** Mauritius, Oberoi Zahra & Madina (Nile cruisers, Egypt), Sahl Hasheesh (Egypt), Indonesia/Bali (Australia-driven), Morocco. Q4 RevPAR +13%; some West Asia overflight benefit (Egypt/Morocco routes avoid Iran).

growth verticals / optionality:

- **OFS scale-up:** growing with domestic airline volume.
- **Renovation-led uplift:** reopenings (Oberoi Grand) act as quasi-new growth without greenfield risk.
margins & cost dynamics:
- EBITDA growth lagged revenue (Q4 cons. +1% vs +10% rev; FY +3% vs +8%) on: (1) **business-mix shift** — higher OFS (lower margin), (2) **wage-code impact** (Rs 30 Cr one-time FY), (3) higher Q4 expenses — airport levy (OFS), repair & maintenance, CSR, legal expenses, donations; other expenses +20% in Q4.
- Margin philosophy: protect guest/team/asset quality; "eliminate waste," not cut costs. FY27 should normalize (FY25 base had lounge-services + Oberoi Grand drag now lapped; OFS margin base found).
- Rate-premium strategy: won't discount ARR to chase occupancy.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- FY26 capex Rs 680 Cr: Mumbai leasehold→freehold land conversion ~Rs 330 Cr; Oberoi Rajgarh Palace ~Rs 125 Cr (commissioned); ~Rs 100 Cr renovations (Kolkata + others); remainder replacement capex.
- FY27 renovations (EIH): ~<90 rooms Oberoi Bangalore (blocks of 18 over summer); Trident BKC F&B revamp (later in year); 4 floors Trident Nariman Point (~6 months, underway); 4 floors Oberoi Bombay (one floor at a time, staggered) — impact managed in lean months, "minimal."

capital allocation:

risks & watch-items:
- **Geopolitics / inbound demand:** West Asia war (from end-Feb) hit foreign room-nights & occupancy in March; higher airfares, fewer routes, Bangalore foreign bookings down. ~50% of Q4 business is foreign — material sensitivity. Mgmt didn't quantify the loss (offset by domestic).

- **Connectivity dependence:** Oberoi Rajgarh (Khajuraho) — only seasonal Delhi flights (none Jul–Sep), constrains occupancy ramp.
- **Supply wave FY29–30:** luxury micro-markets could see occupancy/ARR pressure (mgmt downplays).
- **Execution slippage** on managed contracts (owner-driven) and owned project redesigns (Gandikota, Tirupati).
- **Margin drag** from rising OFS mix and wage code recurring.
- **Udaipur** weddings down YoY.
management quality / tone: Candid and measured. Vikram Oberoi openly admitted not validating the January demand hypothesis, declined to give forward revenue/3–5yr CAGR ("analysts should model that"), and was self-deprecating (apologized repeatedly for misnaming a participant). Emphasized conservative underwriting (IRR/NPV, sensitivities), rate-premium discipline, and protecting quality over cost-cutting. Credible, owner-operator long-termism; transparent about slippages and structural issues at Oberoi Grand. Tone cautiously confident despite a "very challenging year."

themes.title: Hospitality & travel up-cycle
themes.need: Q1FY27 split hotels from airlines. INDHOTEL delivered a 17th consecutive record quarter - consolidated revenue INR 2,419cr (+15%), EBITDA INR 753cr at 31.1%, standalone occupancy jumping to 82% from 76% on a 41.8% standalone EBITDA margin, and asset-light management-fee income INR 168cr (+26%) - with management now framing the West-Asia war as a NET tailwind because outbound travel stays home; leisure RevPAR (Rajasthan/Goa) ran up high-20s. Airlines got the mirror image: INDIGO's EBITDAR margin collapsed from 28.0% to 15.6% on blended ATF of ~INR 140-150/litre versus INR 85-90 pre-war (fuel CASK +~80% YoY), leaving yield as the only defence. MHRIL shows domestic leisure premiumisation is real - Keystone average unit realisation +73% to INR 14.4 lakh on stable gross sales. LEMONTREE/CHALET/SAMHI/THELEELA ride the same occupancy-led room cycle; TRAVELFOOD/TBOTEK/DREAMFOLKS remain levered to airport PAX and B2B travel.
themes.driver: Occupancy-led (not rate-led) RevPAR compounding plus INDHOTEL's Ginger conversion cadence stepping 15->20->25->40 per quarter through FY27; for airlines the swing is INDIGO's guided Q2 PRASK growth of 'more than 25%' on flattish capacity against ATF cracks.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: EIH Limited owns and operates luxury and upper-upscale hotels, resorts and a luxury Nile cruiser under the Oberoi Hotels & Resorts and Trident Hotels brands, plus Maidens Hotel in New Delhi. Oberoi properties target discerning domestic and international leisure and luxury travellers seeking curated, destination-rooted experiences, while Trident serves business and leisure travellers looking for modern comfort and efficient service. The portfolio spans Indian gateway cities, palace/heritage and wildlife destinations, and international locations across the Middle East, Africa, Indian Ocean and Indonesia.

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL)
guidance.body:
- **No forward RevPAR/ARR numbers given** (policy). Levers on existing inventory = (1) drive ARR via premium positioning, (2) eliminate waste (not blunt cost-cutting). Mgmt sees "headroom in ARR if market remains buoyant."
- **Apr–May FY27:** "better than expected," led by strong domestic demand (qualitative only).
- **Demand structure:** domestic luxury propensity rising; India underpriced vs Europe/N. America/Asia at top-end luxury ($1,000+ rates common abroad, EIH "well below"); FX devaluation (~15–20%) pushes Indians to travel domestically — tailwind.
- **Supply view:** most luxury industry supply lands FY29–FY30; mgmt not concerned — uses conservative IRR/NPV underwriting, maintains rate premium rather than discounting; demand-supply gap favorable "next couple of years" (CFO).
- **Capex guidance:** ~Rs 600–700 Cr/yr for next 1–2 years; steps up higher toward FY29–30 as bigger hotels come on. Maintenance/replacement capex embedded.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India is significantly underpenetrated on hotel supply, particularly in the luxury and upper-upscale segments; in many destinations demand continues to outpace the supply of quality accommodation, supporting pricing power
- Occupancies remained broadly stable while average room rates strengthened, resulting in another year of RevPAR growth for the Indian hospitality industry
- Growing diversity of demand beyond established gateway cities towards heritage destinations, wildlife circuits, wellness retreats, pilgrimage centres and leisure markets such as Khajuraho, Kabini, Coorg, Hampi and Makaibari
- Structural demand tailwinds from rising affluence, improving infrastructure, expanding air connectivity and increasing formalisation of the economy
- Sharp expansion at the top end of India's income pyramid is enlarging the addressable market and shifting luxury hospitality from an occasional milestone purchase to a recurring lifestyle preference
- Geographic decentralisation of affluence into smaller cities (Ahmedabad, Surat, Jaipur, Lucknow, Nagpur, Vadodara, Visakhapatnam) is creating new feeder channels across business travel, leisure, destination weddings and MICE
- Policy and connectivity tailwinds: extended Modified UDAN scheme, Seaplane Viability Gap Funding covering destinations in EIH's existing and planned portfolio, PM Gati Shakti, Vande Bharat expansion and proposed high-speed rail corridors
- WTTC ranks India the world's 8th largest travel and tourism economy, with tourism's share of GDP still below potential, leaving headroom for sector expansion
- Near-term headwind: escalation of the West Asia conflict restructured trans-continental aviation routes, roughly doubling airfares on key Europe-Asia routes, with Indian foreign tourist arrivals declining approximately 20% in the months following escalation; India's domestic travel base provides insulation, with inbound weakness concentrated in Agra, Jaipur and Kerala
- Global luxury travel is shifting from amenity-based propositions towards bespoke, culturally embedded experiences, rewarding operators with genuine local depth and service heritage; travellers allocate budget to fewer, longer, more immersive trips, supporting room-rate growth even where occupancy is below peak
- Management notes the operating environment in FY 2025-26 was challenging, with geopolitical tensions, West Asia developments, an extended monsoon and aviation disruption negatively influencing demand at different points in the year
- Managed hotel development pipeline comprises twenty-four hotels with approximately 1,800 keys
- Owned and invested portfolio pipeline includes approximately 825 keys across multiple projects
- Pipeline spans a diverse range of destinations across India and international markets, described as one of the strongest pipelines of new hotels in the Company's history

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: EIH describes itself as at an inflection point with the most ambitious expansion programme in its history: 29 properties are under development across India, the Middle East, Africa and South Asia, a pipeline that will add approximately 2,500 keys by Calendar Year 2030 and broaden both geographic reach and brand coverage. Management frames this as growth that can be delivered without diluting standards, given industry-leading margins and zero net debt. Alongside new-build expansion, the Company continued to invest in asset improvement during FY 2025-26 - depreciation rose because of hotel renovations and the addition of a new hotel property during the year - and the Directors' Report describes the year's capital expenditure outlay (standalone and consolidated) as reflecting continued investments in expansion and asset improvement initiatives. Funding capacity is supported by nil long-term and short-term borrowings as at 31st March 2026 and a CARE AA+ (Stable) issuer rating assigned during the year.

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Renovation drag] Two flagship assets (The Oberoi Grand Kolkata, 209 keys; Trident Jaipur, 132 keys) are under renovation, so reported keys and city-level comparatives are not like-for-like; the deck also notes "Change in RevPAR is inclusive of hotels opened & closed during the respective periods".
- [Geopolitical impact] One city in the Q1 RevPAR-by-city chart is flagged "# Impacted due to West Asia conflict", but the marker's placement is lost in extraction so the affected city cannot be identified from this text.
- [Prior-year exceptional] The comparative quarter carried an exceptional item of (110) INR Cr in both the consolidated and standalone P&L, absent in the current quarter - relevant when reading the headline PAT growth of 224% (consolidated) and 250% (standalone).
- [Deck inconsistency] The cover slide reads "Investors' Conference Call / Quarter ended 30th June 2023" while the covering letter, slide 2 and all tables refer to the quarter ended 30th June 2026 (Q1 FY27); the 2023 cover date appears to be a stale template line.
- [Associate structure] Trident Visakhapatnam is an owned hotel "through EIH Associated Hotels, i.e. an associate company of EIH Limited", so part of the owned pipeline sits outside the parent's direct ownership.
